title: The agent loop
objectives: Build an agent loop with stop conditions and a step cap against a scripted model.

screens.title: One task, traced
screens.prose: An **agent** is a loop: send the messages to the model, run any tool it calls, append the result, and ask again until it answers. Task T03 asks how far DUNM moved from 1 to 15 March 2024. Here is the trace with the scripted model.

params.title: T03
lines: user: [T03] By what percentage did DUNM move from 2024-03-01 to 2024-03-15?

screens.question: How many times is the model called?

feedback.correct: 4: three tool calls, then the answer 4.07%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the model's replies.

byKey.tools: That counts the tool calls; the final answer is a model call too.
byKey.all: That counts every message, the user's and the tools' included.

explain.text: Each model call adds one message; each tool call adds a result. 4 model calls and 3 results, after the question, make 8 messages.

screens.title: Step through the loop
screens.prose: Slide through T03 one step at a time: each step appends one message, the model's reply or the tool's result.
screens.question: After which step does the model first have both closes it needs?

hints.text: The closes arrive as tool results.
The second result comes at step 4.

feedback.correct: After step 4: the second get_close result. Step 5 asks pct_change, step 6 returns it, step 7 answers.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the second tool result.

byKey.first: Step 2 brings the first close only.

explain.text: Step 4 brings the second close. A real model would choose each reply from the results so far; that choice is what makes it an agent rather than a fixed chain, though this scripted one follows a fixed script.

screens.title: Stopping
screens.prose: The loop stops when the model answers. It must also stop when the model never does. Task T10's script repeats one search for ever. With a **step cap** of 6 model calls and no other check, the loop runs to the cap.

params.title: T10, cap 6
lines: user: [T10] Which note is the best match for 'halloran margins profit'?

screens.question: How many tool calls does T10 make before the cap stops it?

hints.text: Every model call here is a tool call.

feedback.correct: 6: one per allowed model call, all identical.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The cap counts model calls, and each is a search.

byKey.cap-minus: Every allowed model call is a search, including the last.

explain.text: Without the cap the loop would run until the case times out; against a paid model it would run up a bill. The cap ends it after 6 calls, status 'max_steps'.

screens.title: Repeated calls
screens.prose: A cheaper stop: if the last 3 tool calls are identical (same name, same arguments), nothing new can come of a fourth. Add that check to the same run of T10, cap still 6.

params.title: T10, repeat check
lines: user: [T10] Which note is the best match for 'halloran margins profit'?

screens.question: How many tool calls does T10 make now?

hints.text: Stop after the third identical call.

feedback.correct: 3, status 'repeated': half the calls of the cap alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Stop once 3 identical calls are in a row.

byKey.cap: That is without the repeat check.

explain.text: The repeat check stops T10 after 3 calls. It cannot replace the cap: a model that varies its calls slightly never repeats exactly.

screens.title: The same task as a workflow
screens.prose: T03's steps are known in advance: two closes, then the change. A **workflow** is fixed code that calls the tools, and sometimes the model, in a set order (prompt chaining and routing are two patterns). Here even the model call can go, since these steps need no judgement: `get_close`, `get_close`, `pct_change`, with no model choosing them.
screens.question: How many model calls does the workflow need to get the number?

hints.text: Who chooses the tools in a workflow?

feedback.correct: None: the code makes the 3 tool calls itself and gets 4.07%. The agent took 4 model calls.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The workflow needs no model to pick the steps.

byKey.tools: 3 is the tool calls; the question asks model calls.

explain.text: A model may still phrase the reply, but the steps are fixed code: cheaper, faster and testable line by line, provided the steps really are known. Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' advises starting there.

screens.title: Results not tied to their call
screens.prose: A harness appends each tool result as plain text in a `user` message, with no tool name, instead of a tool result tied to the call it answers. The scripted model reads results from tool messages, as a real API pairs each result with its call.

screens.question: What should the loop do?

options.text: Stop and record the answer; judging it is a separate step
Refuse the answer until a tool is called
options.why: The loop runs the model; it does not grade it. Some tasks need no tool.

options.text: Ask the model again, hoping for a tool call
options.why: Asking again without a reason is guesswork; record and judge instead.

hints.text: Is answering without a tool ever right?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Is it the loop's job to grade answers?

explain.text: The loop records 56.38 with status 'answer'. Whether it was right, and whether the required tool was used, is scored afterwards against the task.

screens.title: The agent loop
screens.prose:
What you built:

```text
messages = [question]
repeat up to max_steps:
    reply = model(messages, tools)
    append reply
    if reply is an answer: stop
    result = run the call (or its error)
    append result as a tool message
    if the last 3 calls are identical: stop
```

and return every message, so the run can be scored.
screens.question: Which stop must never be left out?

options.why: Useful, but a model that varies its calls slightly never repeats exactly.
Without it the loop would not end on success either, but the cap would still end it.
A timeout helps, but the cap bounds cost in model calls directly.

hints.text: Which stop works whatever the model does?

feedback.correct: The cap: it ends every run, whatever the model does.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which stop cannot be dodged?

explain.text: Only the cap bounds every run; the other stops end common cases sooner.

screens.title: The workflow in code
screens.prose: Write `run_workflow(task, tools)`: the fixed chain for these tasks, with no model at all. It gets the same raw request as the agent, `task['question']`, and reads the ticker, dates and search text from that text with `parse_question`. Return the answer text and the tools called. A tool that raises ends the chain: return `None` and the tools called so far, the failed one included.

explain.text: When the steps are known, the chain is shorter than the agent, needs no model to pick tools, and cannot loop. When a step depends on what the last one found, as T12's holiday does, a fixed chain has no way to recover.

screens.title: An unbounded pipeline
screens.prose: A desk runs an automated research pipeline overnight: a model reads filings and calls tools until it is satisfied. One night a filing triggers an endless series of searches against a paid model API.
screens.question: Which control would have bounded the cost?

options.text: A step cap on model calls per filing
A larger model that loops less
options.why: It may loop less often, not never; nothing bounds it.

options.text: A prompt telling it not to repeat itself
options.why: A prompt guides; only code bounds the loop.
An alert reports the cost after it is spent.

hints.text: Which control works whatever the model does?

feedback.correct: A step cap, plus a repeated-call check to stop it sooner.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which control bounds the loop in code?

explain.text: A cap bounds the cost of every filing; the repeat check would have stopped this one after three identical searches.

ideas: An agent is a loop: send the messages, run any tool call, append its result as a tool message, and repeat until the model answers.
Every loop needs a step cap; a repeated-call check stops common loops sooner, and the loop returns every message for scoring.
When the steps are known in advance, a workflow (fixed code calling the tools) is cheaper, testable and cannot loop; it cannot recover from a step it did not plan for.

formula.name: Stops
formula.note: The cap is the one stop that cannot be dodged.

summary.trap: No step cap, or results not paired with the call they answer, so the model never sees them.
